name: pflua (pflang packet-filter compiler on LuaJIT) vs libpcap BPF interpreter and Linux kernel BPF JITs
baseline: libpcap user-space BPF interpreter (C); also the old 2011 Linux kernel BPF JIT and the 2014 Linux eBPF JIT (C), both adapted to run in user space by the pflua-bench repo
workload: Run pflang (tcpdump filter language) expressions such as 'accept all', 'ip', 'tcp', 'tcp port 5555' and 'icmp' over a saved capture of about 1M ICMP ping packets, measured in millions of packets per second (MPPS), 50 runs per implementation in one process after a discarded warm-up run.
claimed_speedup: README: 'In many circumstances, pflua is the fastest pflang implementation out there, by a long shot.' Medians of the 20 runs in results/ping-flood (derived from page data), MPPS pflua vs libpcap vs linux-bpf vs linux-ebpf: 'tcp' 89.9 vs 37.9 vs 62.2 vs 56.1; 'tcp port 5555' 89.9 vs 37.9 vs 61.8 vs 57.6; 'icmp' 89.9 vs 54.8 vs 83.5 vs 77.7; 'ip' 91.6 vs 68.0 vs 85.3 vs 78.7; 'accept all' 127.9 vs 92.1 vs 109.8 vs 95.4. That is about 2.4x libpcap and 1.4x the Linux 2011 BPF JIT on the 'tcp' filter.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated. pflua embeds LuaJIT (built with make); the libpcap and Linux BPF/eBPF JIT C code are built with make in pflua-bench with no flags given in the README.
hardware: Intel Core i7-3770 (x86-64), Debian GNU/Linux (3.14-2), otherwise unloaded machine (pflua-bench README)
why_faster: Source (pflua README, Performance section): LuaJIT trace compilation emits machine code specialised to the traffic actually seen; pflua can hoist and eliminate bounds checks while BPF must check every packet access; it works in network byte order while BPF converts to host order; it uses LuaJIT's register allocator and optimizer whereas the Linux kernel JIT has a limited optimizer.
stars_or_usage: 312 stars (pflua); 26 stars (pflua-bench); written for the Snabb user-space networking toolkit
tradeoffs: Needs LuaJIT; filters are compiled at run time and the speed depends on LuaJIT trace behaviour; pflua is a filter engine only, not a full libpcap replacement, and the project says there may be bugs or differences against libpcap.
caveats: First-party benchmark by the pflua authors with the compiler flags of the C baselines unstated, so tier C. The compared pflang pipelines use different algorithms (pflua has its own optimizer; libpcap runs an unoptimised BPF interpreter), so this is partly an optimiser win. The README text says about 180 MPPS for the ping flood while the CSV medians show 128 MPPS for 'accept all' and about 90 MPPS for tcp/icmp, so the prose and the raw CSVs do not match exactly. On the real-world wingolog.org capture pflua is sometimes slower than libpcap and the Linux JITs, which the authors blame on LuaJIT trace state-transfer costs. The README notes the ping-flood filters can run faster than the 'accept all' loop, so the harness overhead is not fully separated. Last commit 2017 (pflua) and 2016 (pflua-bench), so numbers are about nine years old.
found_via: WebSearch: 'github LuaJIT OR Java OR JVM outperforms C DPDK OR C implementation packet processing OR database OR codec benchmark JIT faster' led to Igalia/pflua; opened the pflua README, the pflua-bench README and results/ping-flood CSVs (libpcap.csv, linux-bpf.csv, linux-ebpf.csv, pflua.csv)

name: Yao.jl (Julia quantum circuit simulator) vs Qulacs (C++) and QuEST (C) in yardstiq/quantum-benchmarks
baseline: Qulacs 0.1.9 (C++ core, installed as the pip wheel) and QuEST (C, through pyquest-cffi 0.1.1), single thread, full-amplitude state-vector simulation
workload: Single-thread time to apply one X, H, CNOT or T gate and to run a parameterized Rx/Rz plus CNOT-entangler circuit on 4 to 25 qubit full state vectors.
claimed_speedup: No numeric claim in text; the result is a plot. Read from yardstiq/quantum-benchmarks images/pcircuit_relative.png (derived from page data, approximate): at 22-25 qubits the parameterized circuit takes about 1.8-1.9x longer in Qulacs and about 8x longer in QuEST than in Yao. Single-gate plot (gates_relative.png) at 25 qubits: QuEST about 2.4x (X) and 2.5x (CNOT) slower than Yao, Qulacs about 0.9-1.0x (X, CNOT) and about 0.6x (H, Qulacs faster); QuEST about 0.75x on T (QuEST faster), so the single-gate result is mixed.
compiler_and_flags: Julia 1.3.0 (LLVM 6.0.1, ORCJIT, skylake), Yao v0.6.1, JULIA_NUM_THREADS=1, BLAS threads 1 (MKL). Qulacs: 'pip install qulacs', a prebuilt wheel with unstated flags. QuEST: cloned from QuEST-Kit and built by the repo's setup script, flags not stated in what I opened.
hardware: Intel Xeon Gold 6230 @ 2.10GHz (Tesla V100 present but the single-thread CPU runs are the ones read here)
why_faster: The benchmark repo gives no mechanism. Plausible, not stated by the source: Julia JIT-compiles the gate kernels for the exact host CPU (skylake) and specialises them on gate type, while the Qulacs competitor is a generic pip wheel.
tradeoffs: Julia startup and JIT latency; needs a Julia runtime; the benchmark covers state-vector simulation only.
caveats: Benchmark is written and run by the Yao author's group (first-party), the README says its results are only up to date till 2020 (Julia 1.3.0, Yao v0.6.1, Qulacs 0.1.9), and flags of the C/C++ baselines are not stated, so tier C. Yao's script records minimum(t).time from BenchmarkTools while the Qulacs script uses pytest-benchmark; which statistic the plots use was not verified. QuEST goes through pyquest-cffi (Python cffi), so some of its gap may be binding overhead. Qulacs wins on small qubit counts and on the H gate, and QuEST wins on the T gate, so the win is not uniform. The plots are images; the ratios above were read off them by eye. The Yao paper (Quantum 2020) was not opened.
found_via: Recall of Roger Luo's quantum-benchmarks after WebSearch 'github Julia package faster than C++ library benchmark'; opened Yao.jl, yardstiq/quantum-benchmarks README, RESULTS.md, the gates_relative.png and pcircuit_relative.png images and the yao and qulacs benchmark scripts

name: JavaScript JIT engines (Firefox 55 and Safari 11) vs C: Fourmilab fbench
baseline: The C version of fbench built with GCC 3.2.3 -O3 on Linux (the table's reference row, relative time 1); the same table lists G++ 5.4.0 -O3 C++ at 0.939
claimed_speedup: Relative time versus C (lower is faster): Mozilla Firefox 55.0.2 Linux 0.372; Safari 11.0 macOS 0.424, i.e. about 2.7x and 2.4x faster than the C reference (derived from page data). Other engines on the same row: Brave 0.18.36 1.334; Google Chrome 61 1.378; Chromium 60 1.386; Node.js v6.11.3 1.495, all slower than C.
compiler_and_flags: C baseline: GCC 3.2.3 -O3, Linux. JavaScript: Firefox 55.0.2 (Linux), Safari 11.0 (macOS), Chrome 61, Chromium 60, Brave 0.18.36, Node.js v6.11.3; no JIT flags.
caveats: The C reference is a 2003-era compiler (GCC 3.2.3), and the page itself says fbench is far more sensitive to the efficiency of the trigonometric library routines than to general code generation, so this mostly compares libm sin/cos/tan/atan implementations, not compiler quality. The page offers no mechanism for the JS win, and the V8-based engines (Chrome, Chromium, Brave, Node.js) are 1.3-1.5x slower than C on the same benchmark. Machine and CPU are not stated per row, and the C++ row (G++ 5.4.0 -O3, 0.939) shows a newer compiler is only 6% faster than the reference, so a modern GCC with a modern libm might close the gap. Tier capped at C because no mechanism is given. Numbers date from 2017.

name: ZstdSharp (C# port of zstd 1.5.7 on the .NET JIT) vs native libzstd
baseline: Native zstd (C) called through P/Invoke from the checked-in prebuilt x64 libzstd.dll (version and build flags not stated in the repo)
workload: Compress and decompress the 'dickens' text file (src/Zstd.Extern/dickens) at zstd levels 1, 5 and 15, one call per iteration with a reused context, measured with BenchmarkDotNet; native is the baseline row.
claimed_speedup: README BenchmarkDotNet ratios (ZstdSharp time / native time, lower is faster): compress level 1 0.96 (24.111 ms vs 25.034 ms); compress level 15 0.90 (1,987.616 ms vs 2,214.733 ms); compress level 5 1.13 (slower); decompress 1.12 at level 1, 1.09 at level 5 and 1.07 at level 15 (slower). So the C# port is about 4% and 10% faster on compression at levels 1 and 15 and 7-12% slower on decompression.
compiler_and_flags: .NET 9.0.7 RyuJIT, X64 AVX2 (BenchmarkDotNet v0.15.2, .NET SDK 9.0.302). Native libzstd.dll: a prebuilt binary under src/Zstd.Extern/x64, compiler, flags and zstd version not stated.
hardware: 12th Gen Intel Core i7-12700 2.10GHz, 1 CPU, 20 logical and 12 physical cores, Windows 10 22H2
tradeoffs: Managed port that avoids shipping native binaries; the README says best performance needs .NET with System.Runtime.Intrinsics, and .NET Standard or .NET Framework use software fallbacks. The port is mixed: it is faster at some compression levels and slower at decompression and at level 5.
caveats: The source gives no mechanism for the compression wins. The native baseline is a vendored prebuilt libzstd.dll whose zstd version, compiler and flags are not given (the port tracks zstd v1.5.7), so the baseline may be an older or less tuned build than a current -O3 clang or gcc build; hence tier C. Native calls go through P/Invoke (IntPtr marshalling), a small per-call overhead. Only one input file (dickens) and three levels are shown, and the port is slower at decompression, the usual hot path. First-party BenchmarkDotNet run on Windows 10.
